content: Epizootic lymphangitis is an infectious disease affecting the lymphatic system of horses and mules, caused by the fungal pathogen Histoplasma farciminosum. While cattle can also contract the disease, they exhibit a higher level of resistance compared to equids. This condition is distinct from other equine diseases such as glanders and equine lymphangitis. In the United Kingdom, epizootic lymphangitis is classified as a notifiable disease, meaning its occurrence must be reported to authorities. The World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) categorizes it as a List B disease, which includes transmissible diseases of significant socio-economic and public health importance, as well as those impacting international trade in animals and animal products. Reports on these diseases are typically submitted annually. The clinical presentation of epizootic lymphangitis often includes the following symptoms: Skin lesions, primarily located on the legs, though they may occasionally appear on the head or neck and rarely on other parts of the body. Prominent lymphatic vessels in the affected areas, accompanied by the development of small, firm nodules approximately 1 cm in diameter along their course. These nodules eventually suppurate, forming abscesses that discharge a thick, yellowish pus. Over time, granulation tissue (proud flesh) develops at the site of the wounds, with surrounding lymphatic vessels becoming inflamed. The lesions tend to spread progressively. Regional lymph nodes near the affected areas become swollen and indurated (hardened). The ulcers are slow to heal, even with treatment, and may recur after an apparent resolution of the disease. Diagnosis of epizootic lymphangitis is primarily based on the identification of Histoplasma organisms in the purulent discharge. This differentiates it from glanders, as the mallein test, which is used to diagnose glanders, does not elicit a reaction in cases of epizootic lymphangitis. It is also possible for both diseases to coexist in the same animal. Serological testing can be employed as an additional diagnostic tool. This is achieved by culling infected animals and implementing rigorous hygiene protocols to prevent the spread of the fungal pathogen. Vaccination has been used on a limited basis in regions where the disease is endemic, such as Iraq. However, widespread use of vaccination is not currently authorized.
